newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Wage worries dampen Australian rate cut hopes.
newsitem.headline: Wage worries dampen Australian rate cut hopes.

text.p: Australia's central bank on Wednesday dampened expectations of an imminent cut in interest rates, saying in it remained concerned about the inflationary effects of wages growth.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said in its monthly Bulletin for October that some recent wage agreements had been higher than inflation and that a premature rate cut could store up problems for the future.
"Other things equal, a reduction in inflationary expectations would support the case for a reduction in the overnight cash rate," the RBA said.

"Should the economy turn out to be clearly weaker than current projections assume, with likely additional downward pressures on wage bargains and inflation, that case would be strengthened," the bank said.

"On the other hand, on current growth projections, and without evidence that wages are adjusting to the lower inflation environment, a relaxation of monetary policy could have the effect of storing up problems for the future," it said.

Before the comments, economists had widely believed a 50 basis point rate cut was likely after inflation and wages data next week and more likely after the RBA's monthly board meeting on November 5. A basis point is 1/100th of a percentage point.
Bonds yields rose sharply on the news, particularly at the short end of the market, where a 50 basis point easing had been fully priced in ahead of the Bulletin.
Bill futures have been implying a 50 basis point rate cut by the end of calendar 1996 and had begun factoring in another 25 basis point cut by the end of the first quarter of 1997.

Economists said the Reserve Bank's comments suggested an imminent rate cut was not the sure thing the market believed. "It has actually made it a whole lot more difficult (to forecast a cut)," said Colonial State Bank economist Craig James said.

"They want to see further evidence of lower labour costs before they are willing to reduce official interest rates further, so it's certainly not a 'lay-down misere' (sure bet) for a rate cut in November ... It makes it a 50-50 proposition."
UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said he was still forecasting a rate cut, but not with as much confidence.

"Quite clearly the Reserve Bank has some concerns about wages. But providing the average weekly earnings and CPI (consumer price index) report are sufficiently low I don't think they will stand in the way of this rate cut," he said.
"I don't think people should be looking for any more beyond that," Roberts said.
Official cash rates, currently at 7.0 percent, were cut by 0.5 points on July 31 - the first rate reduction in three years.
National Australia Bank chief economist Alan Oster said he thought a rate cut was a line-ball decision, depending on imports data this week and inflation and wages data next week.
"Unless they all go the right way, the Reserve will wait, so I think it's 50-50 (proposition)," Oster said.
Macquarie Bank economist Andrew Ticehurst said that if economic growth forecasts were achieved and there were no signs of wages moderating, the RBA would not cut rates.
"The market has been quite confident that there will be a rate cut, so I think this has set them back a little bit."
The Australian dollar closed slightly higher on the RBA's comments at around US$0.7910, up from $0,7896 at the opening.
The 3-year bond ended with a yield of 6.98 percent, up 13 basis points from its level ahead of the Bulletin release.

The chance of a rate cut appeared to increase earlier in the day when Westpac Banking Corp reported that its October consumer sentiment index fell 4.1 points, or 3.9 percent to 101.4. The index has now fallen 9.2 percent from peak after the March 2 election and is back to its lowest level in a year.
